paper.central_claim: A Claude Code agent (Fable 5), prompted to write code-as-policy with no demonstrations, finds the Push-T simulator, iterates on controller code and reaches 100% success using 46% fewer steps than the best diffusion policy trained with 200 human demonstrations; it extends via a self-generated curriculum to Push-A to Push-Z (99.4%) and to Franka/UR5e simulations with visual feedback.
paper.title: Revisiting the "Push-T" Robot Manipulation Task with Agentic Robotics

signatures.object: Procedural controller code for planar pushing (state-machine with contact library, later MPC plus vision pipeline) authored by a coding agent; baselines: a public LeRobot diffusion-policy checkpoint (200 demos) and a Dubins-pushing controller adapted by the same agent.
signatures.information: Natural-language task prompt, simulator access (the agent finds and reads the gym environment and its source), execution outcomes and failure logs; controller input is privileged state (5-D) or RGB; per-episode task specification at an unstated visibility level; no demonstrations.
signatures.operation: Agent writes a controller, runs it in simulation, diagnoses failures, rewrites it; v3 shifts from search heuristics to MPC with receding-horizon replanning; vision variant adds colour segmentation, IoU pose fitting, calibration and per-push friction adaptation.
signatures.output: A Python controller run with no LLM in the control loop.
signatures.conditions: 2D gym simulation and agent-authored 3D Franka/UR5e simulations; unlimited sim resets; human interaction during 221 hours of agent time.
signatures.feedback: Simulator success/coverage and logs; success is judged by the environment coverage criterion (95% Push-T, 90% letters).
signatures.selection_rule: The agent's own judgement from practice tests (5 episodes on struggling letters) and all-letter exams; no external acceptance gate.
signatures.persistence: Controller code files across 14 iterations in v3 and across rounds v1-v3; human prompts add the vision stage and Push-A to Z.
signatures.later_use: The final controller is evaluated on the same simulator suite and ported to other simulated arms.
signatures.claimed_effect: Push-T: 100.0% (state) / 97.2% (vision) vs 62.5% for the DP checkpoint, mean steps 120.1 vs 223.7; Push-A to Z: 47.1% -> 73.1% -> 99.4%.
signatures.failure_boundary: Simulation only; agent can exploit simulator APIs; sensitive to prompt; cost about USD 1,500-2,000; remaining failures are hard reorientations exceeding the step limit.

signatures.object: Agent-generated Push-Alphabet benchmark and self-generated curriculum.
signatures.information: Simulator source; the agent chooses which letters to practice.
signatures.operation: Agent builds 26 letter environments as subclasses of PushTEnv, then shifts its practice set to currently failing letters.
signatures.output: A benchmark suite and a controller trained against it.
signatures.conditions: Same physics and success rule as gym_pusht, success threshold 90%.
signatures.selection_rule: Exam on all 26 letters after groups of iterations.
signatures.later_use: Final 25-per-letter exam of the same letters.
signatures.failure_boundary: Development and evaluation share letters, simulator and likely seeds; benchmark and verifier are agent-authored.

gap.author_gap: Push-T has mainly served imitation learning; classical and learned solutions need substantial task-specific design or data. The paper asks whether a coding agent can generate a procedural solution and how it compares with demonstration-trained policies.
gap.checked_gap: An exploratory question rather than an identified failure of a named method. The nearest agentic code-as-policy loops (iterative simulator-feedback controller writing) are only cited generically and are not run on Push-T.
lineage: Implicit BC / Diffusion Policy on Push-T
LLM code generation for robot commands
gap.closest_adjacent: Contact-implicit TO and Dubins pushing give model-based solutions; the paper compares only with a Dubins adaptation built by the same agent and with one diffusion checkpoint.
gap.residue: Whether an LLM coding loop can replace demonstration data and hand design for a planar pushing benchmark.
gap.stakes: Demonstration-free controllers for contact tasks with fewer steps.
gap.method_response: Prompt Claude Code to write, test and rewrite controllers in the simulator, extended by a self-generated curriculum.
gap.remaining_gap: Real-world transfer, fair comparison with learned baselines under matched information and effort, held-out letters and seeds, repeated agent runs.
unresolved: No ablation of the loop itself; no run with a different agent or without simulator source access.

tactic_steps_checked: 1 boundary: LLM writes the procedural/MPC solver, execution is in the simulator (met in loose form: the LLM authors the solver instead of delegating to an existing one)
3 loop closure with execution results during construction (met: success/coverage and logs drive rewrites)
4 ablation isolating the load-bearing step (unmet: no one-shot vs loop, no without-source-access run beyond the v1 to v3 trajectory)
success_checks: Typed externally verifiable artifacts: met (executable code scored by the simulator)
Signals obtainable at deployment: partial (the loop uses simulator ground truth that real robots lack)
failure_checks: Benchmark-tailored scaffolding: met as risk (render palette, Push-T family only)
No ablation isolating confounds such as the model's prior knowledge or simulator source reading: met as risk
matches.reason: The learned agent emits a runnable controller whose verifiable output (simulator success) closes the loop mid-construction; this is the C25 operation, with the departure that no sound external solver is reused by delegation, the agent writes one itself.

rs_pattern.reason: decompose_and_delegate/C25 chosen over reframe_as_solvable_object (the paper does not recast Push-T into a solver class; the recast into quasi-static MPC is the agent's output) and controlled_diagnostic_design (the Push-Alphabet suite varies geometry but does not isolate a confound).

executes_pattern.reason: Executable artifact plus simulator-verified loop executed; no isolating ablation.

resolves_problem.reason: No evidence that the demonstration-free controller closes the gap for real-world pushing or that it beats the best learned policy under matched conditions.

revision_proposals: Add a condition under R05: agent has access to simulator source/success checker (reward-integrity risk, E15).

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: C25 executable artifact checked by running it maps to R05's controller program run in simulation trials whose logs drive the rewrite; both close the loop on obtainable execution results.
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions_and_differences: R05 requires trials that are cheap and resettable and a primitive library covering the task: the 2D gym is trivially resettable and the agent writes its own primitives. R05 deploys no model at run time; so does this paper. C25's solver-owned verification is replaced by the simulator's success metric.

claims.text: The agent-written code policy reaches 100% success on Push-T with 46% fewer steps than the best diffusion policy trained on 200 demonstrations.
claims.baseline: One public LeRobot diffusion-policy checkpoint (RGB + pusher position); state-based controller is privileged.
claims.selection_vs_test: Agent developed in the same environment; seed overlap not stated.
claims.result: State controller 100.0%, 120.1 mean steps; vision controller 97.2%, 170.4; DP 62.5%, 223.7 (46% = 120.1 vs 223.7).
counterevidence: Only one DP checkpoint, not 'the best'; privileged-state vs image comparison; steps denominator undefined; development effort not matched.
claims.allowed_conclusion: In gym_pusht a coding agent can produce a controller that solves 97-100% of 200 seeds and needs fewer steps than a public DP checkpoint (62.5%); the comparison is not matched in information, effort or development/test separation.

claims.text: Self-generated curriculum lifts Push-Alphabet success from 47.1% to 99.4%.
claims.setting: 26 letters x 25 episodes, 720-step cap, success at 90% coverage, agent-authored environments.
claims.baseline: Earlier rounds (v1, v2) of the same agent; Dubins pushing with an agent-written adapter (90.2% -> 97.2%).
claims.selection_vs_test: Same letters and simulator used for practice and final evaluation.
claims.result: v1 47.1%, v2 73.1%, v3 99.4%; MPC state 99.4% vs refined Dubins 97.2% with fewer than half the pushes.
counterevidence: Benchmark and verifier are agent-authored; the threshold differs from Push-T; matching of the Dubins adapter effort is not reported.
claims.allowed_conclusion: The loop converges on the agent's own benchmark; not evidence of generalisation to unseen shapes.

claims.text: The controller ports across embodiments (UR5e 98.5%, Franka 89.8% with vision).
claims.setting: Agent-generated 3D simulations of Franka and UR5e with randomized goal poses.
claims.selection_vs_test: The same agent authored and tuned the simulations.

claims.text: The agentic development process costs about USD 1,500-2,000 and 221 hours.
claims.result: 9.5M output tokens; 221 hours under human interaction.
claims.allowed_conclusion: Reported development cost; the human-effort share is unclear.

assessment.evidence_level_note: Closed-loop simulator success on gym_pusht and agent-authored environments; the agent developed on the evaluated simulator, so no transfer; cross-embodiment sims were authored by the same agent.
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: A Claude Code agent with simulator access wrote Push-T controllers that solve 97-100% of 200 fixed seeds in gym_pusht (state/vision), above a reproduced public diffusion-policy checkpoint at 62.5% with fewer mean steps, and reached 99.4% on its own 26-letter benchmark; comparisons are neither information-, effort- nor holdout-matched.
unresolved: Whether seeds/letters used in development overlap with reported ones.
Role of simulator source and web access.

status_reason: Complete text including appendix read; short paper without a related-work or ablation section.

evidence.quote: Results suggest that the agent found the 2D gym simulation online, and used sim experiments to learn push mechanics, iteratively optimizing to achieve 100% success rate using 46% fewer steps than the best diffusion policy trained with 200 human demonstrations.
evidence.support_explanation: Author headline claim, including that the agent located the simulator online.

evidence.quote: The agent iteratively executes the controller in simulation, observes successes and failures, diagnoses model or control errors, and revises \phi .
evidence.support_explanation: Operation: write-run-diagnose-revise loop over controller code; the LLM is not in the high-frequency loop.

evidence.quote: I want you to use code as policy to achieve Push-T. You are not allowed to use a learned policy, but using existing robot data is fine.
evidence.support_explanation: The entire task prompt for the first controller.

evidence.quote: the agent search for the gym simulation environment for Push-T, iteratively generates procedural code, observes execution outcomes, and refines its logic.
evidence.support_explanation: Information: the agent has access to the simulator and its outputs.

evidence.quote: the camera feed undergoes color segmentation against a pre-defined render palette.
evidence.support_explanation: The vision controller is tuned to the simulator's rendering palette.

evidence.quote: We evaluate the publicly released LeRobot Diffusion Policy checkpoint rather than retraining the model.
evidence.support_explanation: The learned baseline is one public checkpoint.

evidence.quote: The evaluated LeRobot checkpoint achieves a 62.5% success rate under the environment’s stringent criterion of at least 95% target coverage, which is comparable to the 65.4% success rate reported by the checkpoint’s official evaluation over 500 episodes.
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline reproduction within 3 points of its official number.

evidence.quote: Diffusion_Policy_LeRobot 62.5% 223.7 6.38 87.4% Claude_state_controller 100.0% 120.1 3.72 96.8% Claude_vision_controller 97.2% 170.4 4.76 94.2%
evidence.support_explanation: Push-T results over 200 seeds: state controller 100.0%, vision controller 97.2%, DP 62.5%.

evidence.quote: An episode is considered successful if the final target coverage reaches at least 90% within 720 control steps.
evidence.support_explanation: Push-Alphabet success threshold (90%) is lower than Push-T's 95%.

evidence.quote: In round v1, a single prompt generated an initial controller achieving a 47.1% success rate.
evidence.support_explanation: Start of the self-improvement trajectory on Push-A to Z.

evidence.quote: In round v3, the agent autonomously inspected failure logs, read the simulation source code to diagnose kinematic bugs on difficult shapes, and shifted from search-based heuristics to an MPC formulation, ultimately achieving a 99.4% overall success rate
evidence.support_explanation: Selection by the agent's own diagnosis, with reading of simulator source.

evidence.quote: Blue dots are practice tests: after each code change, the agent runs 5 episodes on the letters it is currently struggling with
evidence.support_explanation: Selection rule: agent-run practice tests on the same letters it later reports.

evidence.quote: with the agent generating both the environment suite and controller iterations (Figure 1 ).
evidence.support_explanation: The Push-A to Z benchmark is generated by the same agent that is evaluated on it.

evidence.quote: Notably, operating without external web search, the agent synthesized the MPC control logic entirely from its training background.
evidence.support_explanation: The agent found the sim online in the Push-T stage; the MPC stage is stated to have no web search.

evidence.quote: To evaluate it on Push-Alphabet, the coding agent leaves the original algorithm unchanged and constructs an adapter for contact selection, collision-free approach, command conversion, and contact re-engagement.
evidence.support_explanation: The classical baseline's adapter is authored by the same agent.
Cross-embodiment vision results on agent-authored simulations.

evidence.quote: These results provide preliminary evidence that the generated controller is portable across distinct simulated embodiments without modifying its task-level contact reasoning.
evidence.support_explanation: Authors call the cross-embodiment evidence preliminary.

evidence.quote: the coding agent generated about 9.5 million output tokens.
evidence.support_explanation: Cost: 9.5M output tokens, USD 1,500-2,000.

evidence.quote: The agentic development process required approximately 221 hours in Claude “auto mode” under human interactions.
evidence.support_explanation: Wall-clock effort with human interaction; the degree of human steering is not quantified.

evidence.quote: The agent may exploit simulator-specific APIs, state variables, rendering conventions, contact behavior, or numerical regularities that are unavailable or inaccurate on a physical robot.
evidence.support_explanation: Authors concede simulator exploitation risk.

evidence.quote: Results Table 1 reports performance on gym_pusht over 200 fixed evaluation seeds.
evidence.support_explanation: Evaluation seeds for Push-T; overlap with the agent's development runs is not stated.

evidence.quote: We report success rate, final coverage, mean control steps, and mean number of pushes over 25 episodes per letter.
evidence.support_explanation: Denominator for Push-Alphabet: 25 episodes x 26 letters = 650.

evidence.quote: Despite their different formulations, these methods require substantial task-specific effort in algorithm design, optimization modeling, or interaction-data collection.
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap: prior Push-T solutions need task-specific effort.

evidence.quote: We ask: Can AI coding agent generate procedural methods to solve the Push-T task and if so, how do these solutions compare with policies learned from human demonstrations?
evidence.support_explanation: The posed question is exploratory.

evidence.quote: Independently of the observation stream, a per-episode task specification is passed to the controller before the first action, redacted by a visibility level: full (letter polygon, pusher radius, inertia, friction, PD gains), shape (polygon and radius only), or blind (no geometry).

evidence.quote: Push efficiency is measured by the number of discrete pushes required in successful episodes.
evidence.support_explanation: Push count is defined over successful episodes; the headline step reduction is a mean episode length whose denominator is not defined.

evidence.support_explanation: Authors scope the classical baseline's guarantees.

evidence.support_explanation: Prompt sensitivity is conceded.

G.reason: A real contrast (demonstration-based vs procedural) with neighbours named (Dubins pushing, CRISP, world simulator), but framed as an exploratory question; agentic code-as-policy neighbours are not compared and the unmet need is not demonstrated.

M.reason: Prompting a coding agent to write and rewrite controllers in a resettable simulator is a coherent fit for a planar task, and the generated structure (contact library, MPC, friction adaptation) is described, but there is no designed mechanism or testable hypothesis beyond 'the loop works'.

X.reason: The loop is described at the level of rounds and phases with the prompts quoted; selection and acceptance are the agent's own, human interaction over 221 hours is unquantified, the information visibility level is unstated, and code is promised but not provided.

E.measurement.reason: Headline uses the standard gym_pusht criterion on 200 fixed seeds with the baseline reproduced near its official value; Push-Alphabet and cross-embodiment verification rely on agent-authored environments and a lower threshold, with the step-count denominator undefined.

E.causality.reason: The v1->v3 trajectory shows iteration helps on the agent's own suite and a Dubins baseline is run, but no ablation of loop, curriculum, simulator-source access or model; the DP comparison mixes information, effort and development access.

E.holdout.reason: Development and evaluation share the simulator, letters and probably seeds; the agent found and read the simulator; no held-out shapes, no real robot, cross-embodiment sims are agent-authored.

E.statistics.reason: Large fixed-seed episode counts (200, 650) with per-condition tables, but no CIs, a single agent run, and the failure breakdown is one sentence.

E.cost.reason: Output tokens, dollar range and 221 hours are reported openly with a discussion of frontier-model cost; no per-stage costs and resource mismatch with the baseline is disclosed rather than controlled.
